description: Maritime Hacking Village talks from DEF CON 34.

talks.title: Building the Humans Behind the Mission - Talent, Readiness & Cyber Power for US Armed Services
talks.teaser: Military and state cyber leaders discuss how the Navy and Air Force recruit, train, integrate, and keep technical cyber talent.
talks.summary:
This Maritime Hacking Village panel brought together the Principal Cyber Advisors for the Navy and the Air Force, plus a retired Navy cryptologist who later worked on state-level cyber workforce programs. The moderator framed the problem: cyber operations now run through maritime, air, and joint missions, yet the services compete with industry for the same high-end technical people. Panelists said they were speaking for themselves or in their official roles, and that questions would be taken afterward rather than live.

The middle of the discussion covered recruiting and integration. The Navy described lateral transfers of uniformed personnel with adjacent skills such as cryptography and intelligence, along with an aptitude assessment for people without computer science degrees. The Air Force described bringing back warrant officers for cyber and IT, a category it had not used since 1958, and a planned route for hiring people from industry. Joint cyber teams are built to shared standards from the start. On retention, speakers pointed to incentive pay, slow civilian hiring and clearance timelines, and human performance programs for stressed operators. Future skill needs included operational technology, AI and data science, and soft skills such as critical thinking.

The panel closed with state and municipal examples, including community college pipelines and threat-sharing groups, and an invitation to a short undersea cable sabotage war game. The main takeaway was that the services want to move talent in and out of government more easily and to value communication and decision-making as much as technical ability.

talks.title: Why Trusted HMI Engineering Toolchains Remain a Blind Spot
talks.teaser: Shows how HMI engineering tools and their project files create unvetted attack paths into maritime and industrial control supply chains.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the maritime software chain, from equipment vendor to shipyard to classification society to the bridge HMI. The speaker, Younghoon Noh of the maritime security firm CIDR, argues that the engineering tool used to build those HMI applications, and the project files it produces, sit outside the scope of IACS unified requirements E26 and E27. Those requirements test the delivered equipment at approval, but not the tool that consumes project files, so the tool's handling of untrusted input goes unchecked.

The researchers analyzed one HMI builder and reported seven vulnerabilities to KISA through Korea's coordinated disclosure process. The findings fall into four groups: memory corruption while parsing project files from three input formats, which can lead to denial of service or code execution; DLL search path hijacking and loading of unsigned components; silent font installation that can spoof the operator's screen and expose the rendering path; and OPC UA sessions accepted without any security profile, with plaintext fallback. Eunji Choi presented the library loading, font, and transport classes, and walked through a scenario in which a malicious project passes review, gains trust through approval, and then runs its payload on board.

The closing argument is that type approval at delivery does not cover ships that stay in service for decades. The speakers asked for four changes: extend scope to the build tools and the components they load, track vulnerabilities continuously, require a published disclosure policy and an SBOM, and revalidate after security-relevant changes. Full details are to follow once the disclosure window closes.

talks.title: Jamming Spoofing & Spamming - A Tale of GPS Skullduggery
talks.teaser: Explains how GPS jamming and spoofing are detected, geolocated and mitigated, using a January 2026 Los Angeles and Long Beach GNSS disruption as a case study.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a longtime Long Beach harbor pilot, opens by explaining why modern ship handling depends on GPS. Pilot displays overlay live position on electronic charts, along with ship history and projected track. Those displays rely on five inputs: position, heading, rate of turn, course over ground and speed over ground. A bad value in any of them, whether from multipath or interference, leaves the pilot working from wrong information.

He then covers how easy jamming is. Cheap consumer jammers are sold online and are used by some truck drivers to hide from fleet tracking. A sensor placed near container terminals logged frequent but weak jamming events. More capable direction-finding units can tell jamming from spoofing, report signal strength and estimate the bearing to a source. Two such units helped the terminal operators map a jammer's likely location to a nearby road.

The central case is a one-hour disruption on January 29, 2026. At least seven ships, NOAA reference stations and aircraft near the Channel Islands reported GPS anomalies, spoofing or total loss of fix. Public monitoring data pointed to a Navy activity at Point Mugu, which had issued aircraft notices but no ship warnings. The speaker closes by pointing to a recent white paper by Todd Humphreys on Russian GNSS jamming across Europe. His takeaway is that mariners and other position, navigation and timing users should practice operating without GNSS.

talks.title: Maritime Threat Hunting - What We Actually Find When We Look
talks.teaser: Shows what maritime SOC and NOC teams find on vessels and terminals when they inventory networks, hunt threats and turn findings into detections.
talks.summary:
The panelists, who run monitoring and assessments for ships, ports and terminals, opened by saying their hunts rarely began with malware. They began with working out what was plugged in. Network diagrams handed over with a vessel tend to be out of date, since equipment is repaired, retrofitted and temporarily patched, and those patches often stay. Walkthroughs turned up unmanaged access points, personal mobile hotspots that reached both the crew network and corporate systems, and in one case an RFID system running on the guest Wi-Fi.

The talk then moved to operational technology. As ships shift from satellite links to Starlink, some operators have asked to keep navigation-related systems connected for updates. The presenters' answer was to open a path only for an approved window and close it afterward. Their hunting method starts with a defined normal baseline, then correlates identity, host, network, timing and maintenance records against hypotheses such as vendor access outside approved maintenance periods. Every manual finding is then turned into an automated SOC detection, so the next occurrence is caught without a person looking.

The takeaways were practical: asset inventory and segmentation come before advanced detection, drift is a condition that accumulates rather than an attack, and accepted risks should be documented even when they are not removed. Crew-introduced devices were the most common find, and the presenters argued that overly restrictive networks push people toward workarounds.

talks.title: Scuttling Dashboards
talks.teaser: Shows how internet-facing cloud dashboards and control planes can give attackers a path from web bugs to shipboard OT systems and fleet-wide relays.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by explaining scuttling and arguing that maritime digitization is attaching telemetry and IoT devices to ship control systems faster than regulation can follow. The speaker, who runs a maritime security company, says many vessels carry unmanaged connections, and that console passwords are often written down on the bridge or in control rooms.

The middle section walks through several case studies. A cloud-connected monitoring component at an Indian power plant led to access across roughly 3,000 plants after a web application flaw was exploited. On ships, broken authentication and insecure direct object references in a cloud control plane exposed a vessel gateway with hundreds of main engine and steering tags, many of them writable. A second platform that managed shipboard firewalls and satellite terminals allowed attackers to reach vessel networks, and round-robin SOCKS proxies across a few ships could make traffic appear to come from a botnet of hundreds of vessels. An ECDIS chart display was also reachable over RDP with a default credential. The speaker adds that AI agents wired loosely into these APIs and over-provisioned cloud identities widen the same exposure.

The closing point is that dashboards shorten the path from initial access to physical impact, and that none of these cases needed a zero-day. Operators should treat telemetry and remote-command paths as control paths, audit their authentication and object-level authorization, and remove default credentials. The speaker invites attendees to the Maritime Hacking Village, including a CTF that uses a VLCC simulator.

talks.title: LSTM Autoencoder Ensemble for NMEA 2000 Intrusion Detection on Vessel Networks
talks.teaser: Presents an unsupervised LSTM autoencoder ensemble that flags attacks on NMEA 2000 vessel networks without labeled attack data.
talks.summary:
NMEA 2000 is the CAN-based bus that connects navigation, propulsion and safety equipment on boats, yet it has no authentication, so any device can claim any source address. The speaker argues that automotive-style intrusion detection misses quiet, physics-based attacks such as GPS drift, because those stay within normal thresholds. Real vessel captures are rare and labeled attack data is scarce, so the team built a low-cost hardware capture board and a simulated digital twin that emits labeled traffic.

The detector is an ensemble of four LSTM autoencoders, each watching a different facet: message timing, payload statistics, message frequency, and per-device behavior. Each model learns to reconstruct windows of normal traffic, and an alert fires when at least two of the four report high reconstruction error. Thresholds are set automatically at the 99th percentile of validation error, so tuning needs no attack labels. On a 24-hour capture of roughly 9.16 million messages, the ensemble reached an F1 near 0.96 under temporal cross-validation, with about 39 milliseconds of inference latency per window.

The approach also transferred to automotive CAN data. Next steps include fingerprinting the electrical signal of each device, hardening the bus, and collecting data from more vessels and network layouts. The digital twin is planned for public release so others can build their own scenarios, and the audience was encouraged to help find boats willing to share captures.

talks.title: Place Electronic Devices in Maritime Mode - Exposing NTN’s Maritime Attack Surface
talks.teaser: Explains how cellular non-terrestrial networks extend terrestrial mobile threats to ships at sea, and what maritime operators should consider.
talks.summary:
The talk opens from a familiar seafaring habit: once land drops below the horizon, mariners have long assumed their phones stop mattering. The speaker argues that this assumption is weakening. Satellite operators and resellers now market direct-to-device cellular service to yachts, shipping firms, and makers of container trackers, so ordinary handsets and IoT modems can attach to orbiting platforms without specialized hardware.

Next the speaker walks through the 4G and 5G non-terrestrial design. A user device listens for a satellite's broadcast ephemeris, which is unauthenticated, then uses GNSS to pre-compensate for Doppler shift and timing. Beam size, received power roughly 24 dB below terrestrial levels, and the ability to reject devices outside served areas are also covered. The talk then maps familiar terrestrial attacks onto this setting: IMSI catching through a rogue base station, spoofing satellite ephemeris from ground level, abusing a congestion control message to block devices for long periods, and GPS spoofing of a few kilometers to break the connection.

The closing section argues that maritime threat models should treat cellular links as part of the attack surface, and that GNSS dependence now reaches communications too. Operators should inventory which onboard systems depend on cellular modems. The speaker also notes that the maritime sector has little presence in 3GPP, where the only maritime participant found was the lighthouse association IALA. Low-cost NTN IoT development kits were suggested for hands-on study.

talks.title: Shadow Fleets, Cyber Effects, and Plausible Deniability
talks.teaser: Presents a policy-level panel on maritime gray zone operations, covering shadow fleet tankers, GPS spoofing, subsea cable incidents and the cyber side of ocean shipping.
talks.summary:
This panel at DEF CON's Maritime Hacking Village looks at gray zone activity at sea, meaning coercive or disruptive operations below the threshold of armed conflict. The moderator, a former Coast Guard rear admiral with Cyber Command experience, framed the stakes: most global trade moves by ship, so interference with shipping, ports or maritime infrastructure can undermine economics and security without a formal attack.

The panelists argued that the main obstacle is organizational rather than purely technical. IT and operational technology responsibilities are often split, regional and functional teams see the same incident differently, and the people who hold the risk frequently lack the authority to fix it. One speaker described ships and ports as large, poorly documented systems whose unintended behaviors are hard to map, and whose legacy hardware can outlast its vulnerabilities. Sanctions on Russian and Iranian oil were cited as the reason dark tanker fleets grew, and a 2024 cable incident near Finland showed how jurisdictional limits can stall enforcement. A 1990s oil spill law requiring a single responsible owner was proposed as a possible model for cyber liability.

The closing takeaways were to consolidate fragmented data into a clearer picture, assign an accountable leader with a mandate to disrupt threats and restore systems, and tailor responses to the actor's goal, since sanctions evasion calls for different friction than efforts to shift geopolitical boundaries. Panelists also suggested that government software requirements should demand verifiable artifacts and how components connect, not just parts lists.

talks.title: Subsea Cables as Strategic Chokepoints Security, Sovereignty, and the Grey Zone
talks.teaser: Panelists examine how subsea cables, landing stations, and their supply chains could be targeted in grey-zone conflict, and what protection options exist.
talks.summary:
The panel opens by framing undersea cables as a mostly invisible layer that carries most international data and a large share of economic activity, with a direct role in national security. The speakers look past the cable itself to the landing stations where cables come ashore and to the upstream supply chain for optical fiber and repeaters, which demand from AI data centers is straining.

Using Taiwan as a case study, a war-game analysis describes how a handful of high-capacity cables carry most of the island's traffic, and why cutting cables at sea is less effective than striking the land-based landing stations. Shallow-water damage from anchors and fishing gear is the main near-term tool, while deep-sea robotic operations are described as hard to run autonomously. Repairs can take weeks because few repair ships exist and spare cable has long lead times. The discussion then turns to the US, where landing sites cluster in a few coastal areas, and to Alaska, which depends heavily on subsea links.

The closing discussion covers how cable cuts can serve as coercion or signaling, and how attribution is hard when damage looks accidental. Attacks on data centers are raised as a newer kind of target. The panelists argue that governments need shared norms and deterrence options, and that no single fix exists. Audience questions also touched on smart cables with embedded sensors as a possible detection aid, though the speakers said that work is early.
